title: User Error Has Serious Consequences
summary: This page describes situations where interface-induced user error is not a recoverable inconvenience but a source of clinical, industrial, operational, or command-and-control risk. It explains how Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats these contexts through failure-mode identification, domain learning, and performance in reality.
keyFacts: Creative Navy describes high-consequence user error as a design problem defined by specific failure modes, not by general usability measures alone.
IEC 62366-1 is identified as the medical-device usability engineering standard relevant to use-related risk in the Kardion and deSoutter examples.
The Kardion MCS Controller engagement used a prior Emergo by UL formative evaluation with 7 participants and 8 clinical use scenarios under IEC 62366-1 as an evidence foundation.
In the Kardion case, Creative Navy applied a design standard that no element shifts position across any view transition; the standard view required 34 iterations.
The Kardion design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required; FDA approval was determined through Kardion's regulatory submission.
In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon case, eight orthopaedic and trauma surgeons in structured review sessions reported that device state could be verified through brief glances without reading.

In the Gexcon case, configuration errors reduced from 5–8 to 1–2 per simulation, and corrective load reduced from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes; the evidence basis is client-measured across real deployment locations.

In the Raymarine prototype test, wrong-recipient submissions changed from two of eight operators under immediate calling to zero of eight under the confirmation condition, with a cost of 5.85 seconds and about two and a half additional interactions per call.
In the Schone Airspace Group engagement, the wrong-aircraft command was addressed through distinct inspected-aircraft and command-target states, but no measured error reduction was recorded.
In the handheld command-and-control engagement, the recommendation for a dual physical-button commitment gate was not validated, and no accidental activation was measured before or after.

bodySections.heading: User Error Becomes High Consequence When the Downstream Cost Is Not Recoverable
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

User error has serious consequences when an interface-induced mistake is not a recoverable inconvenience. In high-consequence domains, the cost of an error can be patient safety risk, an invalid safety assessment, financial discrepancy at operational volume, a wrong-recipient command, a wrong-object command, or an irreversible commitment.

The design standard in these contexts is not general ease of use. The design standard is the identification of the specific failure mode that the interface must not produce, the interface condition that creates the risk, and the evidence that the design has eliminated or mitigated that condition to an acceptable residual level under the relevant standard or operating context.

bodySections.heading: High-Consequence User Error Changes the Design Standard
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Standard UX evaluation often considers efficiency, learnability, and satisfaction. In high-consequence domains, these measures are necessary but not sufficient. An interface can be efficient under normal conditions and still create use-related risk under abnormal conditions. An interface can be learnable by trained users and still fail when an untrained user encounters it during an emergency.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats the relevant question as failure-mode specific. What does the interface communicate under actual use conditions? What does the interface do when something goes wrong? What interaction patterns, state representations, or visual hierarchies make a specific class of error more likely?

The operating conditions are part of the design brief. A medical-device display may need to be read from 3 metres during a cardiac procedure. A powered surgical device may need to communicate activation state in a brief glance, with gloves, under variable theatre lighting. A point-of-sale interface may need to avoid additional cognitive load at 84 transactions per hour. In these situations, performance in reality matters more than performance under clean test conditions.

bodySections.heading: Medical-Device User Error Is Treated as Use-Related Risk Under IEC 62366-1
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
IEC 62366-1 is identified in this page as the international standard for usability engineering of medical devices. The standard requires manufacturers to identify use scenarios, document use-related hazards, conduct formative evaluation, and demonstrate in summative testing that identified hazards have been mitigated.

Creative Navy has worked in this context on the Kardion MCS Controller and the deSoutter Medical / Zethon surgical device. In both examples, the consequence profile was patient safety under clinical operating conditions. That consequence profile shaped the design standard from the start.

The scope boundary is important. In the Kardion case, Creative Navy produced a usability engineering trail including domain research, formative evaluation, and documented design rationale structured to support Kardion's IEC 62366-1 compliance activities. FDA approval was determined through Kardion's regulatory submission. Creative Navy does not claim compliance as a deliverable.

In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon case, the engagement covered formative evaluation. Summative validation was the manufacturer's responsibility and was not in scope. Creative Navy produced a usability engineering trail structured to support IEC 62366-1 activities; formal compliance is determined through the manufacturer's regulatory submission.

bodySections.heading: Kardion MCS Controller Shows Spatial Stability as a Risk-Control Design Standard
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Kardion MCS Controller manages blood flow in patients undergoing high-risk cardiac procedures and extended cardiogenic shock support. The device is operated by scrub nurses, perfusionists, and ICU nurses under divided attention, with primary attention on the patient and procedure and secondary attention on the controller.

A formative evaluation conducted before Creative Navy's engagement by Emergo by UL involved 7 participants and 8 clinical use scenarios under IEC 62366-1. The evaluation identified specific use-related hazards. Users misread min/max flow values as device-set safety limits rather than readings of actual variation. The startup sequence was longer than clinical expectations. Scrub nurses and perfusionists had different information needs from ICU nurses operating from different physical positions.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addressed these hazards through a structural design standard: no element shifts position across any view transition. The standard was grounded in a specific failure mode. A user managing a patient under time pressure can rely on spatial memory for where information lives; a layout change disrupts that memory at the moment when active search may not be available.

The standard required 34 iterations on the standard view alone. Versions that produced visually striking results by introducing elements that shifted between views were evaluated, tested with users, and rejected as failure conditions. The design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required. This is a regulatory-result statement, not a claim that Creative Navy delivered compliance or caused FDA approval.

bodySections.heading: deSoutter Medical / Zethon Shows Recognition-Based State Communication Under Theatre Conditions
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The deSoutter Medical / Zethon bone cutter operates at rotational speeds from approximately 200 rpm to approximately 85,000 rpm during orthopaedic and trauma surgery. The surgeon operates the embedded GUI in brief glances during live procedures, while primary attention remains on the surgical field and the patient. The non-dominant hand manages the device, the sterile field restricts positioning, and gloves reduce fine touch precision.

The legacy interface followed the internal software architecture. Its information content was correct, but activation states and readiness conditions required reading to interpret. In operating theatre conditions, reading means diverting sustained attention from the patient, creating use-related risk.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method established a design standard in which every critical state had to be interpretable through recognition in a brief glance, without reading. The design used redundant non-colour cues: spatial position, icon form, and reserved colour each independently communicated critical state, so that no single channel failure made a critical state ambiguous.

Six competitor devices were benchmarked during Sandbox Experiments. The common failure pattern was reliance on colour as the primary state indicator. Under ideal theatre lighting, colour as primary can work. Under variable theatre lighting, it does not provide the same reliability. The surviving design did not rely on colour alone for any critical state.

Eight orthopaedic and trauma surgeons in structured review sessions reported that device state could be verified through brief glances without reading, and that parameter adjustments no longer interrupted surgical workflow. The evidence basis is surgeon-reported from design review sessions, not post-deployment operational measurement.

bodySections.heading: Gexcon Shows Deferred Consequence in Industrial Safety Assessment Software
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Gexcon's CFD simulation software is used by engineers performing gas dispersion modelling, explosion risk assessment, and facility safety validation for industrial installations. An interface failure in this context does not necessarily produce an immediate visible incident. A misconfigured scenario can run, produce outputs that look valid, and enter a safety assessment used for facility configuration, emergency planning zones, or operational permissions.

Before Creative Navy's design work, configuration errors per simulation averaged 5–8. Each error produced 4–6 hours of corrective load. The interface did not communicate where in the simulation setup the error had occurred, so engineers had to identify and trace the error against the outputs.

After Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design engagement, configuration errors reduced to 1–2 per simulation, and corrective load reduced to approximately 20 minutes. The evidence basis is client-measured across real deployment locations. The mechanism described in the case evidence is an explicit error-prevention layer in the interaction architecture: requirements specified which values had to remain visible during scenario setup, where warnings were needed, and how the system should respond to incomplete or contradictory input.

The consequence profile appears in the reliability of the safety assessments the software produces. An interface that reduces configuration errors and correction load reduces uncertainty about whether the simulation configuration was valid. The available evidence does not present this as a reported incident-rate outcome.

bodySections.heading: Petrol Shows Procedural Consequence at Transaction Volume
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Petrol's POS system operated at peak rates of 84 transactions per hour. Combined transactions involving fuel, shop, voucher, and loyalty activity created a consequence profile different from patient safety or structural safety.

In this context, individual transaction errors were not individually catastrophic. At volume, those errors accumulated into financial discrepancy, supervisor escalation, and cashier stress. The design standard was operational integrity under a condition where the interface could not add cognitive overhead to a role already operating at maximum throughput.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats this as a high-throughput operational system rather than as a general usability problem. The relevant risk is not a single dramatic failure. The relevant risk is repeated procedural error under sustained throughput.

bodySections.heading: Raymarine Shows Confirmation as a Second Decision Point, Not an Error-Prevention Guarantee
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the Raymarine engagement for the next generation of Raymarine's fixed-mount VHF line, the error class was addressing a digital call to an unintended vessel. Under immediate calling, two of eight operators submitted a wrong-recipient request. Under the confirmation condition, zero of eight did.

The interpretation is narrow. Confirmation did not prevent target selection mistakes. It made the recipient identity legible at a second decision point, giving operators the opportunity to detect and correct the mistake before submitting the request.

The cost is part of the result. The confirmation step cost 5.85 seconds and about two and a half additional interactions per call. Creative Navy designed the test protocols, moderated all twenty-four sessions, and analysed the results; Raymarine supplied the physical bench mockup.

The evidence describes operator behaviour on a prototype against a fixed scenario fixture, with eight participants per round and no significance testing. The evidence is not a population estimate, not a measure of real-world calling accuracy, and not a measure of outcomes at sea. No safety, rescue, or collision outcome is established by this evidence.

bodySections.heading: Schone Airspace Group Shows Wrong-Object Separation With Deliberate Friction
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
The Schone Airspace Group engagement treated the wrong-aircraft command as its central error class. The design response separated the inspected aircraft and the command target as independent variables with distinct visual treatments. The target used a double solid outline and a labelled badge. The inspected aircraft used a dotted outline and a separate badge. Both states could appear at once on the same card.

The rejected alternative was one generic selected state. The accepted cost was that two highlighted identities are visible simultaneously, adding complexity in exchange for clearer separation of operator intent.

Changing the command target requires a named, explicit operator action. That action changes the recipient and sends no aircraft command. The accepted cost is one additional explicit action to operate a different aircraft. This is deliberate friction.

These are design decisions with their costs recorded, not measured error reductions. No claim is made that the design prevents wrong-aircraft commands or reduces operator error. The step from the interface stating the correct fact to the operator acting correctly was not measured. The product is built and in test, not deployed.

bodySections.heading: The Handheld Command-and-Control Engagement Shows an Irreversible Action Behind Physical Commitment
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
In the handheld command-and-control engagement for a European manufacturer of uncrewed systems, including one-way effectors, the error with serious consequences was commitment of a one-way effector.

The documented condition was that a command issued through the interface might not reach the vehicle, and the interface should not create a false impression that it had. Established operator behaviour was to press the control repeatedly until subjectively satisfied. The persistent control served as both command input and manual retry mechanism.

The analysis identified several interface risks. A single touchscreen input is not an adequate commitment gate for an irreversible action because touchscreens are vulnerable to accidental touches, rain and moisture, gloves, vibration, palm contact, wrong selection under stress, and digitizer faults. Symmetrical strike and abort placement at opposite screen edges may imply a physical key mapping that does not exist. A visible and enabled control communicates that the action is always available when availability actually depends on connectivity, operating mode, and vehicle state. Repeated input is not feedback because the operator cannot know whether they are retrying the same request, creating a duplicate, or acting on aged information.

The counter-recommendation, written jointly by Creative Navy's designers and the client's designers, was to keep strike request status visible at all times, avoid exposing strike as a permanently active touchscreen control, commit the strike by pressing and holding both flip-guarded physical buttons simultaneously for a defined duration, and keep abort in a fixed, predictable position only once the system confirms that an action is in progress and remains abortable.

The recommendation did not make the system safe and was not validated. The deliverable records that hold duration and physical-control design required human-factors and system-safety testing that was not performed. No accidental activation was measured before or after. The client did not accept all of the recommendation, and the residual disagreement remains part of the documented case boundary. Creative Navy designed the surface through which a human supervises the system; Creative Navy did not design the system, datalink, effector, or targeting logic.

bodySections.heading: Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design Method Starts With Domain Learning and Performance in Reality
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method addresses high-consequence user error through work that happens before design decisions are made. Domain learning is treated as operational immersion, not background research. The purpose is to understand which interface conditions constitute risk and why.

In the Kardion engagement, Creative Navy began from the Emergo formative study, then ran mental model sessions with cardiologists and nurses to establish clinical logic for information hierarchy that the prior study had not fully mapped. In the deSoutter engagement, Creative Navy reviewed twelve human factors studies on operating theatre performance, gloved-hand interaction, and dual-task conditions under clinical pressure. In the Gexcon engagement, the team became productive users of CFD software by studying manuals, running controlled tests, and attending intensive stakeholder sessions before design decisions were made.

Performance in reality is the corresponding design standard. Interfaces are evaluated under the operating conditions where their failure modes become consequential: from 3 metres during a cardiac procedure, in variable theatre lighting with gloves, while reading a value and moving around a vehicle under workshop conditions, or at 84 transactions per hour during peak load.

IEC 62366-1 requires medical-device manufacturers to identify use scenarios, document use-related hazards, conduct formative evaluation, and demonstrate in summative testing that identified hazards have been mitigated.

The Kardion engagement used a prior Emergo by UL formative evaluation with 7 participants and 8 clinical use scenarios under IEC 62366-1, which identified misread min/max flow values, startup-sequence concerns, and different role-based information needs.
In the Kardion case, Creative Navy applied a design standard that no element shifts position across any view transition, and the standard view required 34 iterations.
The Kardion design passed FDA evaluation as submitted, with no design changes required.
In the Gexcon case, configuration errors reduced from 5–8 to 1–2 per simulation, and corrective load reduced from 4–6 hours to approximately 20 minutes.
weakerClaims: In the deSoutter Medical / Zethon case, eight orthopaedic and trauma surgeons in structured review sessions reported that device state could be verified through brief glances without reading and that parameter adjustments no longer interrupted surgical workflow.

In the Raymarine prototype testing, wrong-recipient submissions changed from two of eight operators under immediate calling to zero of eight under the confirmation condition, with a cost of 5.85 seconds and about two and a half additional interactions per call.

The Schone Airspace Group engagement recorded design decisions and accepted costs for separating inspected aircraft from command target, but did not measure reductions in wrong-aircraft commands or operator error.

The handheld command-and-control engagement recommended a dual flip-guarded physical-button commitment gate, but the recommendation was not validated and no accidental activation was measured before or after.
limitations: The page describes multiple consequence profiles with different evidence strengths; the examples should not be treated as equivalent evidence categories.
Creative Navy does not claim medical-device compliance as a deliverable in the Kardion case; FDA approval was determined through Kardion's regulatory submission.
The deSoutter Medical / Zethon engagement covered formative evaluation; summative validation and formal compliance were the manufacturer's responsibility through the regulatory submission.
The deSoutter surgeon feedback is from structured review sessions and is not post-deployment operational measurement.
The Gexcon outcome figures are client-measured across real deployment locations; the page does not present an incident-rate outcome.

The Raymarine findings describe operator behaviour on a prototype against a fixed scenario fixture, with eight participants per round and no significance testing; they are not population estimates or measures of real-world calling accuracy or outcomes at sea.
The Schone Airspace Group design decisions were not measured as reductions in wrong-aircraft commands, accidents, or operator error; the product is built and in test, not deployed.
The handheld command-and-control recommendation was not validated, did not make the system safe, and did not measure prevention of accidental activation before or after.
